picks.name: The Sustainability Buyer
picks.why_plausible: The brief targets shoppers who care about reducing plastic waste, and this persona lists refillable_products and home_goods among category_affinities with medium price sensitivity and a $92 AOV. They're the core buyer, but skeptical of greenwashing, so the ad must be specific.
lean_into: specific sustainability claims about plastic bottles avoided per refill
transparency about what's in the concentrate
refillable-by-design, not just recyclable
avoid: vague 'eco-friendly' or 'green' language with no numbers
picks.ad_angle: Concrete plastic math: every concentrate refill replaces another single-use bottle you'd have thrown away.

picks.name: The Busy Parent
picks.why_plausible: Household is a named category affinity and this dual-income-with-kids shopper restocks cleaning supplies constantly, matching the brief's replenishment occasion at an assumed $35 first order. Values score is 0 because sustainability isn't their driver, but the household fit is real.
lean_into: family-friendly, keep it stocked without the bulky bottle haul
trusted by other parents
simple to use, no complicated setup
avoid: complicated onboarding or multi-step refill rituals
picks.ad_angle: One small refill restocks the whole house — less to lug, less under the sink, for the household that runs out of everything.

picks.name: The Value-Conscious Shopper
picks.why_plausible: Household and family_products affinities plus high price sensitivity make the value story of concentrate — you stop paying to ship water and buy the bottle again — genuinely persuasive. They comparison shop, and the brief's claim of cleaning as well as major brands is exactly the proof they want.
lean_into: clear value per use versus a name-brand bottle
bundle and refill-pack offers
reviews and performance proof
avoid: luxury-only or vague premium eco positioning
sustainability as the sole reason to pay more
picks.ad_angle: Cost-per-clean: refills beat buying a new plastic bottle of mostly water every month, and clean just as well.

picks.name: The Convenience-First Millennial
picks.why_plausible: Heavy subscription user whose replenishment behavior fits a refill cadence, and the brief's mixed business model can offer auto-ship. They default to whatever is easiest, so refills arriving before you run out is the hook, not the ethics.
lean_into: subscription perks and auto-refill
one-click reorder
compact refills that ship fast and fit anywhere
picks.ad_angle: Never run out and never carry a heavy bottle home: refills show up on schedule, you just add water.

picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: price_sensitivity: low and affinities for clean_beauty and organic_grocery signal someone who reads labels on what she brings into her home, including cleaners. The brief's clean_ingredients value and 'cleans as well as major brands' claim map to her ingredient-transparency and outcome-focused preferences.
lean_into: full ingredient transparency in the concentrate
outcome-focused: it actually performs against the big brands
fewer harsh residues in the home you live in
avoid: science-backed claims the brief can't substantiate
picks.ad_angle: Know exactly what you're spraying: a short, transparent ingredient list that still outperforms the supermarket standard.

plan.summary: Budget leans on Pantrygood's values-driven pantry restock and Hearthstone's sustainability-motivated new-home kitchen buyers, with smaller tests on household-adjacent baskets (Kitchenly, Northbed) and one values-only sustainability test (Cloudfoot); Swiftcart stays out as a cleaning-products competitor and the apparel/beauty/pet tail is excluded for lacking any purchase-moment link.

recommended.name: Pantrygood
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a mid-tier test on price alone, but it misses the purchase moment: this is a subscription pantry restock by shoppers the notes say are already primed for sustainability claims, which is exactly the replenishment basket a refill system replaces.
recommended.rationale: Notes say shoppers are 'Values-driven shoppers. Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' and the site sells organic pantry staples on subscription, so a concentrate refill is the same household-restock decision with the same plastic-waste argument; $35 sits comfortably under the $86 basket.

evidence.quote: Values-driven shoppers. Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

recommended.risk: High-income West/Northeast grocery shoppers may already subscribe to an established refill brand, so incrementality could be limited.

recommended.name: Hearthstone Goods
recommended.tier_reason: Scored off-category because cookware isn't cleaning, but the notes name the exact buyer this brand wants: sustainability-motivated, non-toxic kitchen shoppers setting up a new home — the moment household cleaning supplies get chosen.
recommended.rationale: Notes read 'Sustainability-motivated kitchen buyers. Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase', and a non-toxic cookware or new-home purchase is precisely when someone replaces their plastic-bottle cleaners; $35 is a trivial add-on to a ~$198 basket.

evidence.quote: Sustainability-motivated kitchen buyers. Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase

recommended.risk: Only 2.8M monthly impressions, so volume will be small; gift purchases also mean some buyers aren't shopping for their own home.

test.name: Cloudfoot
test.tier_reason: Category overlap is genuinely zero, but the brief explicitly asks to reach sustainability-identified checkouts and this publisher's own subcategory is 'sustainable' with sustainability messaging in the notes — a values-targeting hypothesis worth one read.
test.rationale: The brief says 'We want to show up where people who already care about sustainability are checking out', and these are urban professionals who just bought shoes sold on 'Comfort + sustainability messaging'; the test is whether that identity alone carries a $35 household purchase.

evidence.quote: We want to show up where people who already care about sustainability are checking out

test.risk: The link is to the shopper's values, not the purchase; a footwear checkout is a poor moment for household replenishment and conversion could be thin.

test.name: Kitchenly
test.tier_reason: The values signal scored zero only because meal kits carry no sustainability tag, but this is a subscription household-replenishment basket for families who cook daily — the heaviest kitchen-cleaning users and an audience already used to recurring deliveries.
test.rationale: Notes describe 'Family and couples households' buying on subscription, so post-cook kitchen cleanup plus an existing recurring-delivery habit is a plausible route to a refill subscription; worth measuring whether packaging-waste messaging lands on an audience the notes call convenience-motivated.
test.risk: Convenience-motivated shoppers may reject a refill system that requires mixing and reordering, and nothing in the notes shows sustainability responsiveness.

test.name: Northbed
test.tier_reason: Scored as weak fit on zero shared values, but the purchase moment is a home refresh: bedding and bath buyers are outfitting the rooms these products clean, and the notes flag strong home cross-sell.
test.rationale: Notes say 'High cross-sell with home and wellness' among design-conscious buyers, and a refillable system with countertop-worthy reusable bottles is a plausible add-on to a bath and bedding order; the uncertainty is whether design appeal alone converts.

evidence.quote: High cross-sell with home and wellness

test.risk: $35 consumable after a $164 textiles purchase is a category jump, no sustainability signal in the notes, and only 3.6M impressions to read.

excluded.rationale: Pet food restock gives no specific reason to buy cleaning refills, and the brand makes no pet-safe claim.

excluded.name: Stride & Stem
excluded.rationale: Sustainability resonates here, but it attaches to $142 footwear for a narrow professional-women audience at 3.2M impressions — too little household signal and too little volume to read a test.

excluded.name: Tailcrate
excluded.rationale: Dog toy and treat boxes; playful voice and no household-cleaning connection.

excluded.name: Studiogrid
excluded.rationale: Booking a fitness or spa appointment is not a product-restock moment.

excluded.rationale: Apparel checkout with low impulse and no household or sustainability signal.

test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $15.75 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $20.48 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.

bid_strategy.rationale: $35 first order (assumed) × 0.45 = $15.75 target CPA: some revenue repeats. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

test_plan.hypothesis: The brief says 'We want to show up where people who already care about sustainability are checking out', and these are urban professionals who just bought shoes sold on 'Comfort + sustainability messaging'; the test is whether that identity alone carries a $35 household purchase.
test_plan.risk: The link is to the shopper's values, not the purchase; a footwear checkout is a poor moment for household replenishment and conversion could be thin.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $15.75 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $20.48 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $15.75 target after 14 days: move it to core.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

launch_summary.summary: $8,500 of the $10,000 budget goes to two core publishers: Pantrygood, where values-driven pantry restock shoppers are already replenishing household goods, and Hearthstone Goods, where new-home kitchen buyers skew sustainability-motivated. The remaining $1,500 splits evenly across three tests: Kitchenly and Northbed ask whether household-adjacent baskets carry a $35 refill purchase, and Cloudfoot asks whether sustainability identity alone converts without a related purchase moment. Four ads run; The Convenience-First Millennial ad is paused after failing review twice.
uncertainties: The $35 first order value is assumed, and both the $15.75 target and $20.48 maximum cost per new customer are built on it.
The 45% allowable ratio stands in for real margin and repeat-purchase value, which the advertiser has not supplied.
Cloudfoot's shoe checkout links only to shopper values, not to a household purchase moment, so conversions there could be thin.
questions: What does a typical first order actually cost, including starter kit plus refills?
What margin and repeat-purchase value should the cost per new customer be based on?
Are subscription refills available at launch, or one-time purchases only?
